summary: Help children aged 5–8 practise asking genuine science questions and recognising that different questions call for different ways of answering: observing, a simple fair test, researching (book/internet), or asking an expert. The core skill is generative (producing real how/why/what-if questions) plus routing (choosing a sensible method) plus discrimination (telling an investigable question from an opinion/value question that evidence can't settle). The five activities below are a question-sorting workbench that ends with the child's own questions, a task that sharpens a vague wonder into an answerable question, a sort of science-versus-opinion questions, a spoken conversation with a curious scientist, and an optional curiosity-priming scene. Each has its own role, and any sorting of pre-written cards is only a quick check that comes after the child makes up questions.
misconceptions: Thinking a science question always needs an experiment, when observing or researching may fit better.
Confusing a question with a guess/answer ('I think it's the heat') instead of an open question.
Believing every question can be answered by looking it up (or, conversely, by testing).
Treating only 'why' questions as scientific, overlooking 'what if' and 'how' questions.
Asking questions that can't be investigated (opinion or unanswerable) without noticing the difference.
Seeing question-asking as a sign of not knowing, rather than as the engine of science.

activities.title: Question Workbench: sort each wonder into how you'd answer it
steps: Collect a wall of wonder-cards, e.g. 'Does the snail come out when it rains?', 'What do owls eat?', 'Which paper towel soaks up the most water?', 'Why is the sky sometimes red?'
Sort each card into one of four answering methods: WATCH (observe), TEST (try a fair test), LOOK IT UP (research a book/internet), ASK SOMEONE (an expert).
Say aloud, for each card, why that method fits — e.g. 'What do owls eat?' goes to LOOK IT UP because you can't easily watch owls at night.
Notice when the SAME curiosity could become a different kind of question depending on how you'd find out.
Generate at least three of your own wonder-cards and route them too.
activities.insight: A scientist doesn't just ask a question — they also ask 'how would I find out?'. Different questions are answered in different ways, and recognising the method is part of the question.

activities.title: Sharpen a floppy wonder into an answerable question
steps: Start with a vague wonder such as 'Why is the sky like that?' or 'Why is the snail slow?'.
Use comparison words (more, than, when, which, redder) to reshape it into something you could actually check — e.g. 'Is the sky redder in the EVENING THAN the morning?'.
Explain what you would observe or compare once the question is sharpened.
Try sharpening one more wonder of your own.
activities.insight: A vague wonder becomes an investigable science question when it points to something specific you can observe or compare.

activities.title: Which questions can science settle, and which can't?
steps: Sort a short mix of questions into 'we could find out' versus 'people would just disagree', e.g. 'Do woodlice go to the damp side?' versus 'Are woodlice the nicest minibeast?'.
Name the feature that decides it: evidence can settle one, but the other is a matter of opinion or taste.
Come up with your own question about an animal or object that science could NOT settle by investigating.
Discuss what you would trust if a book disagrees with what you observe (e.g. the book says woodlice like damp but the garden ones keep going to the dry side), and how you could settle it.
activities.insight: Scientific questions are the ones evidence can answer; opinion and value questions can't be settled by observing or testing, no matter how hard you look.

activities.title: Wonder together with a curious scientist (spoken dialogue)
steps: Look at a shared picture or real object (a puddle, a snail, a shadow) and wonder aloud about it.
Respond when the curious partner asks 'could we find that out by watching or testing, or would we need to look it up or ask someone?'.
Finish each wonder by naming HOW you would answer it (watch / test / look up / ask).
Take a turn asking the partner a question too.
activities.insight: Talking a wonder through out loud with someone can help you sharpen it and pick a way to answer it.

activities.title: Curiosity-priming scene (optional warm-up)
steps: Explore a rich scene with tappable or pointable curiosities (a puddle, a snail, a shadow).
For each one, notice a model question and a suggested 'how could we find out?'.
Use what you notice to start your own questions before the workbench or conversation.
activities.insight: There are things worth wondering about everywhere, and each wonder can be paired with a way to find out.

checkQuestion: You wonder whether the woodlice in the garden like damp places or dry places. Talk me through it: how could you find out the answer? Is there more than one way to find out? And is there any question about woodlice you could NOT find out by investigating?
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning offers a way to gather evidence — set up a choice with a damp side and a dry side and watch where the woodlice go — and recognises there are several routes to an answer (observe them in the wild, do a fair test, ask an expert, read a book), choosing the one that suits the question. Crucially the child can name a question science cannot settle by investigating — a matter of opinion or value such as 'are woodlice the nicest minibeast?' — showing they grasp that scientific questions are the ones evidence can answer.
